---
title: "Get started"
---

## Installation

Install from GitHub, or clone the repository to run the examples locally.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Python

```bash
python3 -m pip install "git+https://github.com/Larsvanderlaan/causalCalibration.git#subdirectory=python"
```

For plotting, install the optional dependencies with `python3 -m pip install matplotlib`.

### R

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
  "Larsvanderlaan/causalCalibration",
  subdir = "r/causalCalibration"
)
```

For `method="isotonic"`, also install `reticulate` and the Python package `lightgbm`:

```r
install.packages("reticulate")
reticulate::py_install("lightgbm")
```

If you use an existing Python environment, configure `reticulate` to use the environment where `lightgbm` is installed.

### From source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Larsvanderlaan/causalCalibration.git
cd causalCalibration
python3 -m pip install -e 'python[plot]'
```

From the same directory, install the R package:

```r
install.packages("r/causalCalibration", repos = NULL, type = "source")
```
:::

## Prepare the inputs

The package calibrates predictions from a treatment-effect model you have already fitted. Each row needs a prediction, a binary treatment indicator, an observed outcome, and nuisance estimates for the chosen loss.

| Input | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `predictions` | One treatment-effect prediction per observation |
| `treatment`, `outcome` | Treatment coded as `0` or `1`, and observed outcome |
| `mu0`, `mu1` | Estimated conditional outcome means under treatment `0` and `1`; required for `loss="dr"` |
| `propensity` | Estimated probability of treatment `1` given covariates; required for both losses |
| `outcome_mean` | Estimated conditional outcome mean given covariates; required for `loss="r"` |
| `fold_predictions` | For cross-calibration, an `n × K` matrix with predictions from each fold-specific model |
| `fold_ids` | Optional fold indices, numbered `1` through `K`, identifying each row's out-of-fold prediction |

Use cross-fitted nuisance estimates when possible. In a randomized trial, you can supply the known treatment probability as `propensity`.

## Fit and predict

Start with `loss="dr"` when you want calibration for the original population and overlap is adequate. Use `method="isotonic"` for a nondecreasing step function. See [Losses and methods](choosing-losses-and-methods.html) for alternatives.

The examples below assume `tau_hat` contains predictions on a calibration sample that was not used to train the treatment-effect model. All other fitting inputs refer to those same observations. `tau_new` contains predictions for new observations from the same treatment-effect model.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Python

```python
from causal_calibration import fit_calibrator

cal = fit_calibrator(
    predictions=tau_hat,
    treatment=a,
    outcome=y,
    mu0=mu0_hat,
    mu1=mu1_hat,
    propensity=e_hat,
    loss="dr",
    method="isotonic",
)

tau_calibrated = cal.predict(tau_new)
```

### R

```r
library(causalCalibration)

cal <- fit_calibrator(
  predictions = tau_hat,
  treatment = a,
  outcome = y,
  mu0 = mu0_hat,
  mu1 = mu1_hat,
  propensity = e_hat,
  loss = "dr",
  method = "isotonic"
)

tau_calibrated <- predict(cal, tau_new)
```
:::

If your model was trained with cross-fitting, follow the [cross-calibration guide](cross-calibration.html) to use the full sample without setting aside a calibration split.

## Check calibration

Use `diagnose_calibration()` to estimate remaining calibration error, obtain a confidence interval, and compare raw and calibrated scores. All predictions, outcomes, treatment indicators, and nuisance estimates must refer to the same evaluation observations. See [Diagnostics](diagnostics.html) for examples and interpretation.

`assess_overlap()` summarizes propensity-score tails and effective sample sizes. Its recommendation can help you choose between the original and overlap-weighted populations; the screening cutoffs are practical defaults.
